node.description: Historian of contemporary Quebec and Montreal who joins urban development, economic relations and ethnic diversity. In the Prix du Québec interview he rejects a single-factor portrait of a rural, homogeneous French Catholic society and emphasizes the intertwined forces shaping Quebec. The collaborative Histoire du Québec contemporain places modernization in longer social change; its joint authorship remains explicit.

named_group_routes.relationship: Labroussian economic and social history at Laval
named_group_routes.evidence_note: Savard (1974) says Ouellet owed a debt to Labrousse and Chaunu; Robert Mandrou prefaced Ouellet’s 1966 book (review heading). Dechêne trained in France in the Annales milieu of Mandrou and Goubert before her Paris doctorate (1973), published as Habitants et marchands (1974) (Charron, Dictionnaire universel des créatrices; formal supervision not asserted). Linteau (1983) says social history began in Quebec in the 1960s under Annales influence but that his generation was shaped more by French and Quebec sociologists and American historians. Specific contributions to the Laval and New France strands, not an Annales origin for Quebec historiography.

named_group_routes.relationship: The modernist generation adopts social history
named_group_routes.evidence_note: Linteau (1983) describes his cohort adopting social history and serial sources (censuses, civil registers), becoming more quantitative, and widening the subject from French Canadians to Quebec’s whole population. Self-description of one generation.

named_group_routes.relationship: The metropolis–hinterland approach, taken up by Canadian urban historians in the 1970s and then contested by them (1954–85)
named_group_routes.evidence_note: His own statements. The 1954 article proposes the metropolis and its hinterland as a field of study, including 'social and cultural associations' as well as economic ties (pp. 17–18), and names Masters's The Rise of Toronto as the closest application (p. 17). In 1981 he writes that 'urban history' grew within regional writing because cities 'are also centres that focus and structure regions or sub-regions about them. The interplay of city and region thus demands and has received attention', and that he had 'always sought to emphasize the reciprocal and complementary nature of the relations between the great city and the territory it dominates' (Manitoba History no. 1, web text). Davis (1985) lists his urban-history articles: 'Urban Development in Canada', Urban History Review 1 (1974), and 'Metropolis and Region', Urban History Review 3 (1979) (nn. 6, 11; unread). In-period reception, from Davis, Urban History Review 14:2 (1985), read in full: 'In the 1970s metropolitanism helped preside over the birth of a new sub-discipline, urban history', and according to Artibise and Linteau (1984) the articles by Careless on metropolis and region 'marked, in some ways at least, the self-conscious beginning of urban history' in Canada (p. 96; a quoted-in witness); urban historians 'have remained the most faithful to the metropolitan concept of J.M.S. Careless, the godfather of their subdiscipline' (p. 96); Gilbert Stelter called the metropolitan thesis in 1977 'the most significant approach to Canadian urban history' (p. 96, quoted). A contribution, contested within the field: Davis argues that 'there is no single metropolitan thesis' (p. 107), that Careless's approach 'has fallen into desuetude in historical circles' (p. 103), that Artibise found the metropolis/hinterland concept 'not really a theory that explain[ed] Canadian urban development' (p. 103, quoted), and that urban historians 'might do better by abandoning the metropolitan approach altogether' (abstract, p. 95). Davis also records Careless's own reserve: he would 'disclaim and deny such a metropolitan “thesis”' (p. 96, quoting 1973). This is a Canadian contribution; it does not claim that Dyos's or US urban history drew on Careless. edge_800 (urbanhistory → cdn_national_tradition, critique) stays: it records the field's rejection of metropolitanism, this edge the field's use of it.
named_group_routes.map_label: Metropolis and hinterland in Canadian urban history, 1954–85

named_group_routes.relationship: Ouellet's critiques of two interpretations: the Montreal school's Conquest thesis (Séguin's 'décapitation' of a national bourgeoisie, taken up by Brunet), with the habitant's trauma placed in the failing agrarian system rather than the Conquest (1962–85); and parts of the post-1960 generation's economic history, organised in his reading, in 'une grande partie' of it, around French-Canadian inferiority and the independence movement, whose revisions of Séguin's thesis Linteau, Robert and Normand Séguin followed (1985)
named_group_routes.evidence_note: The Montreal school. His own texts. 1962 (with Hamelin, read): French-Canadian historiography reflects 'les réactions émotives des classes dirigeantes canadiennes-françaises', and its simplifications result 'à la fois du mépris de l'économique et de l'idéalisation du fait politique' (p. 32; no historian is named). 1976 (read): 'Si notre « habitant » a subi un traumatisme, ce n'est pas au moment de la conquête mais au moment où le système agricole traditionnel ne peut plus fonctionner comme autrefois' (p. 116). 1985 (read): 'pour Maurice Séguin, théoricien de l'École néo-nationaliste', the leadership of New France belonged to the bourgeoisie, 'de sorte que la décapitation s'était exercée sur l'élite nationale elle-même' (p. 18); 'Cette thèse avait été épousée par Michel Brunet dès les années 1950'; in the 1970s 'la thèse de la dégradation de la bourgeoisie avait besoin d'être dédramatisée', and 'Ces retouches au modèle de Maurice Séguin furent faites par Gilles Paquet et Jean-Pierre Wallot, en particulier' (p. 19); at the core of the crisis controversy stood 'la thèse néo-nationaliste enrichie de l'idée de modernité' (p. 25). In 1984 (recorded by the 1.136 Creighton packet, not re-read here) he asked whether the scheme of Séguin, Frégault and Brunet was 'bien différent' from Creighton's post-Conquest 'société semi-féodale décadente' (p. 227). In-period Montreal reader: Tousignant (1980) on 'la profondeur du fossé qui séparait Fernand Ouellet de l'école néo-nationaliste de l'Université de Montréal et de son maître à penser, le professeur Maurice Séguin' (p. 419), and, as Tousignant reports, Ouellet had 'raillé le schéma d'interprétation freudien de l'école néo-nationaliste de Montréal à propos du «choc» de la Conquête' (p. 423); the text Tousignant refers to was not identified or read. Séguin has no entry, so the edge targets the montreal_school strand. The modernists. His own text, 1985 (read for pp. 11–29 and the pages named): the dominant preoccupation of most of those who built the new economic history 'était par trop centrée sur la situation précaire des Canadiens français en Amérique du Nord', a feeling 'pas étranger à la montée du mouvement indépendantiste québécois'; the themes of dependence, of Quebec's lag behind Ontario and of francophone inferiority 'imprègnent d'une façon ou d'une autre une grande partie de cette historiographie', and 'ces préoccupations ont entraîné les historiens à négliger des secteurs entiers de l'histoire économique et, par conséquent, à se fermer nombre de voies d'accès à une explication du social' (p. 18); after Paquet and Wallot's 'retouches au modèle de Maurice Séguin' (p. 19), 'On peut en dire presque autant des études de Jean-Claude Robert, de Paul-André Linteau et même de Normand Séguin sur le caractère dynamique de la bourgeoisie foncière rurale et urbaine' (pp. 19–20). The same 1985 survey also credits the period with the emergence of a more scientific social history; the passages above are its critical ones, and their limits ('une grande partie', 'presque autant') are kept. In-period reader: Rudin's characterisation, not Ouellet's: Rudin (1995, ¶9–10) describes Ouellet's 1985 and 1988 texts as 'une condamnation virulente de l'historiographie québécoise récente' that associates the revisionists with the 'mouvement indépendantiste des années 1970'; Rudin himself (1995b, p. 66) places Ouellet's emphasis on 'mentalités' beside his own. Limits: the 1988 English version and the 1991 essays Rudin also cites are unread; Ouellet's survey is a long review of the field, and the critical passages read are those quoted. One arrow carries both because they share endpoints and type; the strands are montreal_school and modernist_synthesis.

sources.title: J. M. S. Careless, "Frontierism, Metropolitanism, and Canadian History," Canadian Historical Review 35, no. 1 (1954): 1–21.
sources.citation: J. M. S. Careless, "Frontierism, Metropolitanism, and Canadian History," Canadian Historical Review 35, no. 1 (1954): 1–21.

verification.note: Article unread; no abstract available. The metropolitan argument is described here only at title level and through Davis 1985's account of metropolitan theses. Checked against: Crossref DOI record (CHR 35:1, March 1954, pp. 1–21); reprints in One West, Two Myths II (University of Calgary Press, 2007) via Crossref; OpenAlex description of Careless at Work (selected essays) names frontierism and metropolitanism as a main preoccupation. Addendum 2026-10-14: Read in full (pp. 1–21) for the 1.135 person entry in the Internet Archive scan of the issue (sim_canadian-historical-review_1954-03_35_1; OCR checked against the page image for p. 16). The earlier description through Davis is superseded. Quoted: 'frontierism' named 'for want of a more precise term' and the frontier thesis 'proper' never adopted 'as fully or dogmatically in Canada' (p. 1); schools 'merely for convenience' (p. 2); 'the Environmentalist School, or North Americans All' (p. 5); its members and 'no tight determinism is intended' (p. 6, n. 6); Turner's 'open frontier, the hither edge of free land' (p. 6); 'environmental determinism at its most forthright' and the defenders of Turner (p. 7); 'a certain tendency to fix values' (p. 12); overvaluing native and material forces (pp. 13–14); 'a wider framework' (p. 14); the Laurentian 'metropolitan rather than a frontier viewpoint' and 'virtually to establish “metropolitanism”' (p. 16); the metropolis defined and the 'feudal chain of vassalage', Masters and Gras (p. 17, nn. 30–31); 'the other side of the coin to frontier expansion', 'thus is Turner answered', the frontier 'a dependent' (p. 18); 'a metropolitan determinism' and the Clear Grits, Toronto and the Globe (p. 19); frontierism 'borrowed from the United States' (p. 20); 'restates old problems', 'has had its use and its day' (p. 21). Davis (1985) cites the 1967 reprint in Approaches to Canadian History, pp. 78–79.

sources.citation: Donald F. Davis, "The 'Metropolitan Thesis' and the Writing of Canadian Urban History," Urban History Review 14, no. 2 (1985): 95–113.

verification.note: Abstract read: there is no single metropolitan thesis but several approaches; urban historians would do better to abandon the metropolitan approach for its indeterminacy about relations between classes. Checked against: Crossref DOI record with French abstract (Érudit). Addendum 2026-10-14: Read in full (pp. 95–113, text and notes) for the 1.135 person entry, in the Érudit PDF. Quoted: 'Conceived in part as an obituary for the frontier thesis of Frederick Jackson Turner'; 'few other journal articles have been more widely cited or more frequently quoted' (p. 95); Berger's 'the programmatic statement of the metropolitan approach' (pp. 95–96; n. 1 cites Berger in Canada Since 1867, 1977, pp. 87–88); metropolitanism and 'the birth of a new sub-discipline, urban history'; Artibise and Linteau (1984): 'the self-conscious beginning of urban history'; Careless 'the godfather of their subdiscipline'; Stelter (1977): 'the most significant approach to Canadian urban history'; Careless (1973): 'I would disclaim and deny such a metropolitan “thesis”' (p. 96); five approaches, Careless's the 'ecological'; Lower 'some eight years before' (p. 97); W. L. Morton's objection, quoted from 'Canada's History and Historians' (p. 98, n. 19); Careless's own account of his debt to Gras, from a letter of 11 July 1983 (p. 101, nn. 47, 51); 'a relatively sterile hybrid', 'of only limited usefulness', 'fits the mould of “consensus” history' (p. 102); 'fallen into desuetude', Artibise's 'not really a theory', 'weak on causality; it is more taxonomic than explanatory' (p. 103); S. D. Clark at the 1974 CHA meeting (p. 107); Careless on Turner on television (p. 109). The 'near-doctrinal status' remark (p. 96) is from a private letter (n. 2) and is not used. [creighton draft: Read in full for the 1.135 Creighton entry (Érudit PDF via the Internet Archive capture of 26 September 2024; UHR 14:2, October 1985, pp. 95–113). Careless's 1954 article 'conceived in part as an obituary for the frontier thesis of Frederick Jackson Turner' (p. 95); Harrison (1981, p. 25) quoted: Creighton 'probably the first to advance a metropolitanist interpretation, although the closely related "staples" thesis had been put forward by Innis much earlier'; Morton's 'Clio in Canada' (1980 reprint, p. 107) quoted: Creighton emphasized 'the preponderant role commercial monopoly and centralized business have played'; Morton ('Canada's History and Historians', reprint pp. 34–35) quoted: the metropolitan thesis, which he associated with Creighton and Careless, 'seems necessarily to minimize the importance of the hinterland' (pp. 97–98); Careless said he drew 'neither from Creighton or Innis' but from medieval social history and N. S. B. Gras, and melded Gras with 'the Laurentian School, then regnant' (p. 101). Morton's texts themselves are unread.]

sources.title: J. M. S. Careless, “Limited Identities — Ten Years Later,” Manitoba History, no. 1 (1981).
sources.citation: J. M. S. Careless, “Limited Identities — Ten Years Later,” Manitoba History, no. 1 (1981). The first James A. Jackson memorial lecture. Online text, Manitoba Historical Society.

verification.note: Read in full on 2026-10-14 in the Manitoba Historical Society's online text (no page numbers; quotations are unpaginated). The editor's note says the lecture inaugurated the James A. Jackson memorial lectures and reflected on ten years since the 1969 article; the text refers to the 1978 Cook bicentennial as 'last year' and to 'the close of the 1970s', so it was given in 1979. The society's page dates the issue 1981; Buckner (2000, p. 9, n. 16) cites it as Manitoba History 1:1 (1980), p. 7. Passages used: the 1969 summary ('had tended to bulk larger ...') and the quotation of its p. 10; the farmer 'in the midst of a flood'; 'I scarcely caused the flood'; n. 1, 'I did not invent the term “limited identity”, but acquired it from an article by Ramsay Cook ... essentially a commentary on his initial idea'; the quotation from the 1973 working-class bibliography; urban history and 'the interplay of city and region'; 'Metropolitanism is not the antithesis of regionalism. Each is inherent in the other'; 'diversity Unlimited'; 'limited identities remain crucial subjects for the historian's regard — but they should not limit his own perception'; 'cut the sight-lines through'. n. 8 credits Cook (1977) with anticipating 'the next stage for “limited identities”'. Addendum 2026-10-14: Re-read for the 1.138 Kealey draft. Careless quotes the introduction to Primary Sources in Canadian Working-Class History, 1860–1930 (1973, p. 11), 'prepared by Russell Hann, Gregory and Linda Kealey and Peter Warrian': 'For some time J. M. S. Careless has called for … a historical appreciation of the varieties of "limited identities" that constitute Canada', and its aim 'to create a new local history'; he calls working-class history 'one of the most active and productive areas' in the study of limited identities, and says class identities 'must be treated in their national scope'. Kealey (1988, pp. 2–3) quotes the flood passage, dating the lecture 1980. Addendum 2026-10-25: [Response audit: Response-edge audit, separately scoped fresh check. rea_roots_cook_careless: Fresh selected opening and footnote read; existing full-reading and dating qualifications preserved. Locators: Manitoba Historical Society web text, opening andfootnote 1. ]

English version: The Socialization of Quebec Historiography since 1960 (Toronto: Robarts Centre for Canadian Studies, 1988; not seen).

verification.note: Read: pp. 11–29, 38, 47, 51–52, 64–68 and the abstract, from the Érudit PDF (scanned; local French OCR; pages fixed from the running heads); the rest skimmed by name search only. Quoted: until 1963 Quebec historiography 'restée, dans l'ensemble, politique et cléricale' (p. 13); for 'Maurice Séguin, théoricien de l'École néo-nationaliste', leadership of New France belonged to the bourgeoisie, 'de sorte que la décapitation s'était exercée sur l'élite nationale elle-même'; economic inferiority as a preoccupation 'pas étranger à la montée du mouvement indépendantiste québécois', which led historians 'à négliger des secteurs entiers de l'histoire économique' (p. 18); 'Cette thèse avait été épousée par Michel Brunet dès les années 1950'; in the 1970s it 'avait besoin d'être dédramatisée'; 'Ces retouches au modèle de Maurice Séguin furent faites par Gilles Paquet et Jean-Pierre Wallot, en particulier' (p. 19), followed 'presque autant' by Robert, Linteau and Normand Séguin (p. 20); the crisis controversy began 'en 1966 à la suite de la publication de notre Histoire économique et sociale du Québec', with 'la thèse néo-nationaliste enrichie de l'idée de modernité' at its core and the peasant as '«paysan indépendant», sensible au marché et libéré'; Le Goff 'soutint en conclusion l'idée de l'existence d'une crise agricole dès le début du XIXe siècle' (p. 25); Dechêne 'n'a pu faire autrement que de prendre position' (p. 26); on the Patriotes, 'Les mêmes polarisations émergent' among Bernard, Bernier, Bourque, Dubuc, Ouellet and Ryerson (p. 51, n. 128 citing J.-P. Bernard, ed., Les Rébellions de 1837–1838, 1983); 'Fernand Dumont et Jean Hamelin jouèrent un rôle capital d'animation' (p. 67).

sources.title: Fernand Ouellet, “Le mythe de « l’habitant sensible au marché ». Commentaires sur la controverse Le Goff–Wallot et Paquet,” Recherches sociographiques 17, no. 1 (1976): 115–132.
sources.citation: Fernand Ouellet, “Le mythe de « l’habitant sensible au marché ». Commentaires sur la controverse Le Goff–Wallot et Paquet,” Recherches sociographiques 17, no. 1 (1976): 115–132. doi:10.7202/055711ar.

verification.note: Read in full (pp. 115–132) from the Érudit PDF (scanned page images; local French OCR checked against the running heads). Quoted: the habitant defined as 'un paysan traditionnel ayant, au début du Régime britannique, un niveau de pratiques agricoles inférieur à celui de la majorité des paysans européens'; denies calling the eighteenth-century peasant 'morbidement conservateur' (p. 115); from the early nineteenth century 'le paysan, au lieu de transformer ses façons de faire, se durcit et résiste aux pressions en faveur de la rénovation du système agricole'; 'Si notre « habitant » a subi un traumatisme, ce n'est pas au moment de la conquête mais au moment où le système agricole traditionnel ne peut plus fonctionner comme autrefois'; nationalism born 'parmi les professions libérales' and spread 'dans les milieux paysans sous l'effet de l'apparition du problème agricole et des pressions démographiques'; Wallot and Paquet 'ont réduit notre analyse à un simple rapport entre nationalisme et malaise agricole'; their 'problèmes de lecture' made the debate 'presque stérile'; Le Goff's intervention drew attention 'sur la vulnérabilité de la thèse Wallot et Paquet' (p. 116); 'Notre analyse, contrairement à celle des professeurs Wallot et Paquet, porte sur le long terme' (p. 117); exports 1793–1802 vs 1803–12, 'soit un déclin de 30%' (p. 117); 'Si l'habitant avait été aussi sensible au marché que le prétendent les professeurs Wallot et Paquet' (p. 119); Le Goff's doubts about the revenue series 'légitimes et fondées' (p. 129); 'Le débat ne mérite plus d'être poursuivi; c'est la recherche qui exige de l'être' (p. 132). The note's n.* (p. 115) dates Le Goff's CHR article 1973 and Paquet–Wallot's RHAF article pp. 239–270; Crossref gives 1974 and pp. 185–237. Locator reconciled at release (1.138) with evidence-quebec.md §2c, which was written from the printed pages: the long-term sentence is p. 117. The PDF could not be re-fetched (Érudit bot check) to re-verify.

verification.note: Read in full (pp. 415–436) from the Érudit PDF (text layer). A review essay on Le Bas-Canada 1791–1840 (1976). Quoted: Ouellet combined quantitative series and 'la voie «sociologique» réduite au modèle weberien d'une typologie différentielle des mentalités', which 'lui a valu d'être porté aux nues, notamment dans les milieux universitaires anglophones'; 'le Fernand Ouellet de l'Histoire économique et sociale du Québec faisait écho aux vieux préjugés de l'historiographie canadienne-anglaise tout imprégnée de l'idéologie de supériorité de la race anglo-saxonne'; the approach 'qui justifiait la notion désormais dépassée du «retard des mentalités» n'apparaît plus au premier plan dans Le Bas-Canada. C'est une notable amélioration'; the crisis thesis subjected to 'un sérieux «examen critique»' by Paquet and Wallot (p. 416); 'Le choix de cette coupure n'est évidemment pas innocent' (p. 417); the 1966 book reproached the peasantry 'son enlisement dans la routine' (p. 418); 'la profondeur du fossé qui séparait Fernand Ouellet de l'école néo-nationaliste de l'Université de Montréal et de son maître à penser, le professeur Maurice Séguin'; 'Il ne saurait plus être question de porter au seul compte d'une différence de mentalités l'appauvrissement progressif de la majeure partie de la paysannerie' (p. 419); 'Lancé sur la voie de l'approche psychanalytique' after having 'raillé le schéma d'interprétation freudien de l'école néo-nationaliste de Montréal à propos du «choc» de la Conquête' (p. 423); 'Le professeur Ouellet nourrit de telles préventions contre le parti patriote' (p. 430); closing credit to 'une formalisation théorique' that gives 'une intelligibilité vivante' (p. 436, after Nicole Gagnon).

verification.note: Read: a generation born about 1945 and trained at Laval and Montréal in the late 1960s wrote ‘une histoire différente’; it concentrated on c. 1850 to the present to understand industrial, urban Quebec; moved from the history of French Canadians to the history of Quebec’s whole population; social history began in Quebec in the 1960s under Annales influence, but the cohort was shaped more by French and Quebec sociologists and American historians; serial sources; Marxism challenged it but few adopted it fully. Linteau stresses a break around 1970. Checked against: OpenEdition text of the reprint (source note gives Liberté 147, 1983, pp. 34–47); Crossref DOI for the chapter.

verification.note: Metadata only; the two 1962 publications share the title. Bodies unread. Checked against: Crossref DOI records (Érudit, CHA Report 1962; Persée, Études rurales 1962, doi:10.3406/rural.1962.1028). Addendum 2026-10-14: Read in full (CHA Report 41:1, pp. 17–33) from the Érudit PDF (scanned; local French OCR; pages fixed from the running heads) for the Ouellet person entry. Quoted: 'la détérioration rapide de l'agriculture bas-canadienne après 1802 prouve le caractère superficiel des conquêtes antérieures. Dès le début du 19e siècle, la tendance majeure se renverse' (p. 20); 'la routine paysanne, la pauvreté des moyens de transport, les habitudes de consommation de l'habitant canadien-français et l'incompréhension des politiciens expliquent la lenteur des départs et des progrès'; 'Aussi la révolution de 1837-38 apparaît-elle, en grande partie, comme une réponse détournée aux problèmes posés par l'action conjointe des tensions démographiques et de la crise agricole' (p. 31); 'deux entités culturelles sans aucun doute distinctes mais offrant une grande disparité dans leur degré d'évolution. C'est pourquoi le professeur Creighton a pu parler, en se référant à la société canadienne-française, de société féodale décadente'; 'c'est moins la diversité des valeurs que la différence des niveaux d'évolution qui fut la source fondamentale des conflits raciaux'; 'Ce n'est pas que cette crise soit le seul moteur des événements de cette époque troublée'; nationalist historiography's simplifications result 'à la fois du mépris de l'économique et de l'idéalisation du fait politique' (p. 32). The Études rurales version (1962) was not read.

verification.note: Read the opening and summary: ‘révisionnistes’ of the 1970s portrayed Quebec as developing like other Western societies, stressing urbanization, industrialization and class and downplaying ethnic, linguistic, religious and rural distinctiveness; a needed correction of the nationalist narrative that swung too far; a call for a ‘post-révisionniste’ balance. Names Linteau, Robert, Rouillard, Normand Séguin, Durocher, Young, Greer and Dickinson among the revisionists, and Ouellet as a critic of them.
